text: Hydrogen peroxide, H O , can be oxidised to give oxygen, O . This reaction happens rapidly in the
presence of acidified potassium manganate(VII), KMnO .
2MnO (aq) + 5H O (aq) + 6H (aq) → 2Mn (aq) + 5O (g) + 8H O(l)
You will determine the concentration of a solution of hydrogen peroxide. You will first dilute the
solution and then carry out a titration using acidified potassium manganate(VII), KMnO .
FA 1 is aqueous hydrogen peroxide, H O .
FA 2 is 0.0200moldm potassium manganate(VII), KMnO .
FA 3 is 1.0moldm sulfuric acid, H SO .

text: In Question 1, hydrogen peroxide was oxidised to form oxygen. Hydrogen peroxide can also be
reduced to form water. This occurs, for example, when hydrogen peroxide, H O , reacts with iodide
ions, I (aq), to form iodine, I (aq).
H O (aq) + 2H (aq) + 2I (aq) → I (aq) + 2H O(l)
The rate of this reaction can be measured by adding acidified hydrogen peroxide, H O , to a mixture
of iodide ions, I , thiosulfate ions, S O , and starch indicator. As the iodine is produced, it reacts
immediately with the thiosulfate ions and is reduced back to iodide ions.
I (aq) + 2S O (aq) → 2I (aq) + S O (aq)
When all the thiosulfate has reacted, the iodine then turns the starch indicator blue-black. The rate
of reaction may be determined by timing how long it takes the reaction mixture to turn blue-black.
In this experiment you will measure two reaction times and use one of these to calculate the
concentration of the thiosulfate ions in FA 6.
FA 3 is 1.0moldm sulfuric acid, H SO .
FA 4 is the diluted hydrogen peroxide, H O , you prepared in 1(a).
FA 5 is 1.0moldm potassium iodide, KI.
FA 6 is aqueous sodium thiosulfate, Na S2O .
